raw_text:
The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to preserve the survival benefit of defibrillator therapy while avoiding transvenous leads, the component most vulnerable to infection, venous occlusion, tricuspid-valve injury and late mechanical failure. The rationale is grounded in the efficacy of ICDs for primary and secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death [1–3], and in the recognized morbidity of conventional systems, particularly after replacements, upgrades, and long dwell times [4–7].

The S-ICD consists of a lateral thoracic pulse generator and a parasternal subcutaneous electrode. It senses a far-field electrocardiogram, applies morphology-based discrimination, and delivers high-energy shocks without entering the heart or vasculature. The first human experience established feasibility of sensing and defibrillation without endocardial hardware [8]. Subsequent early cohorts showed high conversion efficacy and acceptable implant safety across broader real-world populations [9–13]. The pivotal investigational device exemption study confirmed effective arrhythmia detection and shock termination, with complications predominantly confined to pocket or wound problems rather than intravascular events [14].

Patient selection remains central. The ideal candidate has an ICD indication but no need for chronic bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization, or antitachycardia pacing (ATP). This includes many young patients, those with inherited arrhythmia syndromes, difficult venous access, prior device infection, or high lifetime lead-risk exposure [12,15,16]. Conversely, patients with monomorphic ventricular tachycardia likely to respond to ATP, advanced conduction disease, or resynchronization indications are usually better served by a transvenous or emerging extravascular pacing-capable strategy. Pre-implant electrocardiographic screening is mandatory because myopotential, low-amplitude QRS, or prominent T waves can predispose to oversensing; screening studies demonstrated that a minority of candidates fail morphology criteria, with higher failure in some cardiomyopathies and abnormal repolarization patterns [17,18].

Inappropriate shocks were an important early limitation, mainly from T-wave oversensing, supraventricular tachycardia, low-amplitude signals, and noise. Programming dual zones, using higher conditional-zone thresholds, careful vector selection, and enhanced sensing algorithms substantially reduced this burden [19–21]. SMART Pass filtering further improved real-world specificity without apparent loss of sensitivity [22]. Implant technique also evolved: the two-incision approach and intermuscular generator placement improved cosmesis, stability, and wound outcomes while avoiding the superior parasternal incision [23]. Infection management is generally simpler than with transvenous systems because there is no endovascular lead; extraction is usually less complex, and systemic infection appears less frequent [24].

Comparative data have clarified the trade-offs. Matched observational analyses suggested fewer lead-related complications with the S-ICD but more non-ATP-treated ventricular tachycardia shocks in susceptible patients [25]. The EFFORTLESS registry demonstrated durable safety and appropriate therapy over mid-term follow-up, with complication rates decreasing as operators gained experience [26]. The randomized PRAETORIAN trial showed non-inferiority of the S-ICD to transvenous ICDs for a composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks, while confirming the expected pattern: fewer lead-related complications but absence of ATP [27]. UNTOUCHED, focused on primary-prevention patients with low ejection fraction and contemporary programming, reported low inappropriate-shock rates, supporting the S-ICD as a mainstream option rather than a niche device [28]. The ATLAS randomized trial reinforced the perioperative advantage of avoiding transvenous leads in patients at elevated lead-related risk [29]. Longer-term EFFORTLESS results support stable performance through several years, although generator longevity, body habitus, and future pacing needs remain practical concerns [30].

Current practice therefore frames the S-ICD not as a universal replacement for transvenous ICDs but as a complementary platform. Its main strengths are avoidance of intravascular hardware, lower exposure to lead failure, and suitability for younger or infection-prone patients. Its main limitations are lack of bradycardia pacing, resynchronization, and ATP; larger generator size; need for ECG screening; and potential for sensing-related shocks. Future directions include integration with leadless pacemakers for ATP or bradycardia support, improved discrimination algorithms, smaller generators, and better individualized prediction of pacing need. For appropriately selected patients, the S-ICD is now an evidence-based defibrillator strategy that shifts the risk profile away from the vasculature and myocardium while maintaining effective protection from sudden cardiac death.
